title: The Debt I Refuse to Collect
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] My father left when I was nine, and for two decades his existence was, to me, largely theoretical, a name my mother mentioned only when pressed.
Narrator: He resurfaced three years ago, frail and diminished, having exhausted whatever version of independence he'd once preferred to the family he'd abandoned.
Narrator: [carefully] I won't pretend the reunion stirred anything resembling warmth. What I felt, mostly, was a cold, clarifying kind of obligation, entirely separate from affection.
Narrator: Friends who knew the history seemed almost disappointed when I began managing his medication and paying his rent, as though I owed him nothing and should act accordingly.
Narrator: [reflective] Their disappointment, I think, mistook forgiveness for the point, when the actual reasoning had nothing to do with forgiving him at all.
Narrator: I haven't forgiven him, not in any tidy sense the word usually implies, and I'm no longer certain I owe anyone that particular resolution.
Narrator: [honestly] What I decided, instead, was that his failures were his own account to settle, and caring for him now was mine, and the two ledgers needn't be reconciled.
Narrator: It would be more satisfying, narratively, to say I did this purely for some abstract principle, untouched by anger. That would also be a lie.
Narrator: [gently] Some visits, I sit in the car afterward, furious at him in ways twenty years hasn't dulled, before walking back in the next morning regardless.
Narrator: The regardless is the part that matters, I've decided, not the absence of feeling but the refusal to let feeling dictate the whole of my conduct.
Narrator: [calmly] I'm not owed his gratitude, and mercifully, he rarely offers any performance of it, which spares us both an exchange neither of us could make honest.
Narrator: I do this, ultimately, because becoming someone who withholds kindness until it's been earned felt like a smaller, meaner person than I'm willing to become.
